Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources I've gathered.

---

# Genesis 32 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1: *"Jacob also went on his way, and the angels of God met him."*

**Traditional reading:** After Laban's departure, Jacob journeyed south from Galeed/Mizpah toward the Jabbok. The "angels of God" (literally "messengers of Elohim") met him — not chance travelers (as some Jewish interpreters suggested), but actual angels. The timing is significant: this came after Jacob separated from Laban, suggesting that separation from worldly influences often opens eyes to God's care. The appearance was likely designed to assure Jacob of divine protection before his meeting with Esau. Whether this was a waking vision or a dream is debated; Jacob's two prior visions were at night (Gen 28:12; 31:10).

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html

**Reformed/Baptist (Spurgeon, via Enduring Word):** Spurgeon noted: "Our Mahanaims occur at much the same time… Jacob was entering upon a more separated life. He was leaving Laban and the school of all those tricks of bargaining and bartering which belong to the ungodly world." He also said, "I do not ask that you may see angels… Is not the fact of God's presence better than the sight of the best of his creatures? Perhaps the Lord favored Jacob with the sight of angels because he was such a poor, weak creature as to his faith."

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

---

## v. 2: *"When Jacob saw them, he said, 'This is the camp of God.' So he named that place Mahanaim."*

**Traditional reading:** "Mahanaim" means "two camps" or "two hosts." The best interpretation is that it refers to Jacob's own company and the heavenly host — Jacob realized he was in a "double camp," not alone. Others suggest two bands of angels (one before, one behind) or simply a multitudinous host. Mahanaim later became an important city in Gad's territory (Josh 13:26; 2 Sam 2:8).

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

---

## v. 3–5: Jacob's message to Esau.

**Traditional reading:** Jacob sent messengers (note the contrast with the "messengers of Elohim" in v. 1) to Esau in Seir/Edom. His message was carefully humble — he called Esau "my lord" and himself "your servant." This language may reflect Eastern courtesy, a desire to conciliate, personal contrition for past wrongs, or fear. By listing his wealth, Jacob signaled he wanted nothing from Esau, only reconciliation. He sought "to find favor in your sight."

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

**Baptist (Matthew Henry, via biblehub.com summary):** Jacob's message showed he did not insist upon the birthright. "Yielding pacifies great offences" (Eccl 10:4). We must not refuse to speak respectfully.

- URL: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/32.htm

---

## v. 6: *"When the messengers returned… 'he is coming to meet you — he and four hundred men with him.'"*

**Traditional reading:** The messengers reported only Esau's approach with 400 men — no verbal response from Esau. The 400 men indicated Esau had become a powerful chieftain. Esau's intentions were ambiguous: some commentators see personal vanity or a desire to honor Jacob, others see hostile intent or at least a wavering state. Jacob interpreted it as a threat.

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html

---

## vv. 7–8: *"In great fear and distress, Jacob divided his people into two camps…"*

**Traditional reading:** Jacob's fear was rooted in guilt — he could stand boldly before Laban (where he was in the right) but cowered before Esau (where he was in the wrong). The phrase "greatly afraid and distressed" literally means "it was narrow to him" — he was hemmed in, perplexed. He divided into two camps so that if one was attacked, the other might escape. The commentators note Jacob should have remembered God's promises and the angelic camp just revealed, but his fear overwhelmed his faith.

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html

**Baptist/Reformed (Spurgeon via Enduring Word):** "Jacob had just been delivered from Laban, but he was oppressed by another load: the dread of Esau was upon him. He had wronged his brother; and you cannot do a wrong without being haunted by it afterwards." Guzik adds: Jacob "forgot about God's two camps and tried to make his own two companies." Spurgeon contrasted Abraham's simple, childlike trust with Jacob's scheming: "Abraham never descended to any of the tricks by which Jacob sought to increase his flocks."

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

**Older Anglican (Ellicott):** Jacob's extreme distress, despite repeated divine encouragement, shows his faith was "very feeble; but it was real, and therefore he sought refuge from his terror in prayer."

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html

---

## vv. 9–12: Jacob's prayer.

**Traditional reading:** This is the first recorded prayer in Scripture (JFB). It is universally praised for combining humility, boldness, simplicity, and faith. Jacob addresses God as the covenant God of Abraham and Isaac, then as the LORD who personally commanded him to return. He confesses profound unworthiness ("I am less than all the mercies"), recalls crossing Jordan with only a staff, pleads for deliverance from Esau using the vivid phrase "mother upon children" (proverbial for complete extirpation), and holds God to His promise: "You have said, 'I will surely make you prosper…'"

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/32.htm

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik, Enduring Word):** Jacob's prayer "was humble, full of faith, full of thanksgiving and God's word." Guzik emphasizes that Jacob prayed God's own promises back to Him. Spurgeon (quoted): "When God gave his promise, he did, as it were, put himself in the power of those who know how to plead the promise."

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

---

## vv. 13–21: Jacob's gift to Esau.

**Traditional reading:** After praying, Jacob assembled an enormous gift: 200 female goats + 20 males, 200 ewes + 20 rams, 30 milk camels with young, 40 cows + 10 bulls, 20 female donkeys + 10 males — 550 animals total. He sent them in separate droves with intervals ("breathing space") between them, instructing each servant to say, "They belong to your servant Jacob… a gift to my lord Esau… Jacob is behind us." Jacob's stated motive: "I will appease him" — literally, "I will cover his face" (a legal term later used for atonement, Lev 9:7). He hoped Esau would "lift up my face" (grant favorable reception).

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** Jacob's elaborate gift strategy reveals he went right back to his old scheming after praying. "After all, if Jacob really trusted God, he would be at the head of the procession to meet Esau, not at the back." Guzik compares this to believers who sing "I surrender all" but really mean, "I surrender all the goats… all the sheep… all the camels…" — what Jacob still refused to surrender was himself.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

**Spurgeon (Baptist/Reformed, via Enduring Word):** "What care he takes about the whole affair! We cannot blame him, under the circumstances, yet how much grander is the quiet, noble demeanour of Abraham, who trusts in God, and leaves matters more in his hands!"

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

---

## vv. 22–23: Crossing the Jabbok.

**Traditional reading:** During the night, Jacob rose and took his wives, maidservants, and eleven sons across the ford of the Jabbok (now Wady Zerka, a rapid stream flowing into the Jordan near Shechem), along with all possessions. Scholars debate whether Jacob stayed on the north or south bank after sending everyone across; Ellicott argues he remained on the south side, alone in the ravine — the ideal place for a solitary struggle. The Jabbok's name (from *bakak*, to empty/pour forth, or *abak*, to wrestle) may be a prolepsis pointing to the wrestling.

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html

---

## v. 24: *"So Jacob was left all alone, and there a man wrestled with him until daybreak."*

**Traditional reading:** The verb *abak* (wrestle) occurs only here and was likely chosen for its resemblance to "Jabbok." The "man" is identified by Hosea 12:4 as an angel, and by Jacob himself (v. 30) as God. Most traditional commentators identify Him as the Angel of the Covenant — a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ (Christophany).

**Key interpretive issue — who initiated the wrestling?** The text says "there wrestled a man with him" (not "Jacob wrestled with a man"). The man initiated the conflict. God was the aggressor, seeking to break Jacob's self-reliance.

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** "Jacob didn't wrestle with the Man. Instead, a Man wrestled with him. Jacob would have been happy to have been left alone, but God wanted something from him. God wanted the sacrifice of all of Jacob's proud self-reliance and fleshly scheming, and God came to take these, by force if necessary." Guzik identifies the Man as Jesus in pre-incarnate form. Spurgeon: "We call him 'wrestling Jacob,' and so he was; but we must not forget the wrestling man — or, rather, the wrestling Christ."

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

**Devotional/Evangelical (Griffith-Thomas, Precept Austin):** The wrestling was "an endeavor on God's part to break down Jacob's opposition, to bring him to an end of himself… There is no lesson at all on prevailing prayer. Far from it; quite the opposite. The self-life in Jacob is to be overcome, the old nature is to be conquered." Griffith-Thomas insists this was a literal physical struggle (the outcome in vv. 25, 31, 32 proves it), though the physical was subservient to the spiritual.

- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis_devotional_commentary_2

**Reformed/Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper):** Piper portrays it as God initiating the wrestling to draw Jacob out of his fearful preoccupation with Esau. "Jacob began the night believing his greatest need was to escape from Esau. He ended the night believing his greatest need was to trust in the blessing of God's promise." God sometimes wrestles us "until you're desperate enough to say, 'I will not let you go unless you bless me.' It is a great mercy to be brought to the point where you're desperate enough to insist on what you need the most."

- URL: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/i-will-not-let-you-go-unless-you-bless-me
- URL: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/will-you-wrestle-with-god

**Debate — literal or visionary?** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes: "Many think that as the narrative makes no mention in express terms either of sleep, or dream, or vision, it was a real transaction; while others, considering the bodily exhaustion of Jacob, his great mental anxiety… as well as the analogy of former manifestations… have concluded that it was a vision [Calvin, Hessenberg, Hengstenberg]."

- URL: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/32.htm

---

## v. 25: *"When the man saw that he could not overpower Jacob, he struck the socket of Jacob's hip and dislocated it as they wrestled."*

**Traditional reading:** The Man "could not overpower" Jacob only in the sense that the match appeared even — God could have won at any moment with supernatural power. The hip socket was "touched" (not struck violently). This was a disabling blow that ended Jacob's ability to wrestle using his own strength. The dislocation was real and lasting (see v. 31–32).

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

**Precept Austin (Griffith-Thomas):** God "took away the very power required for wrestling, brought him by one swift blow to the very end of his resources, and left him utterly powerless. Thus Divine love dealt with him in mercy and taught him, albeit in severity, the one lesson he needed most to learn." God could have done this earlier but wanted Jacob's willing surrender first.

- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis_devotional_commentary_2

**Reformed Baptist (Desiring God):** "Why the hip? In part, because God purposes to help Jacob fear his word more than the threats of an angry brother. And so, the night before Jacob's encounter with Esau, God faithfully afflicts him so he can't flee again out of fear of man, but instead is forced to trust God's faithfulness."

- URL: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/in-faithfulness-you-have-afflicted-me

---

## v. 26: *"Then the man said, 'Let me go, for it is daybreak.' But Jacob replied, 'I will not let you go unless you bless me.'"*

**Traditional reading:** The request to depart at daybreak was an acknowledgment of defeat — the Man yielded the victory. At this point Jacob recognized his opponent was divine and shifted from wrestling to clinging. No longer able to fight, he held on with desperate tenacity, seeking blessing. Hosea 12:4 adds that "he wept, and sought favor from Him."

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html

**Precept Austin (Griffith-Thomas):** "From cunning to clinging, from resisting to resting — this was the literal and symbolical experience of the crafty but now conquered Jacob… He is conscious at last of the futility of all his efforts to appease Esau… At last he is in the right position, but at what cost!"

- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis_devotional_commentary_2

**Pentecostal (Guzik):** "Jacob was reduced to the place where all he could do was to hold on to the Lord with everything he had. Jacob could not fight anymore, but he could hold on. That is not a bad place to be." Jacob's real enemy was not Esau outside but his own carnal, fleshly nature within.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

**Reformed Baptist (Desiring God):** "God even afflicted Jacob with a debilitating injury. This had the effect of making Jacob even more vulnerable to Esau, forcing Jacob's faith to more fully rest on God and not himself. If necessary, God will cause us to limp to increase our faith."

- URL: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/will-you-wrestle-with-god

---

## vv. 27–28: *"'What is your name?'… 'Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed.'"*

**Traditional reading:** The question "What is your name?" forced Jacob to confess his identity as "Jacob" — heel-grabber, supplanter, deceiver. The new name "Israel" (*Yisra'el*) is interpreted in two main ways: (1) "Prince of God" (from *sarah* = to rule, be chief), adopted by Calvin, Ainsworth, Murphy, and the KJV margin; or (2) "Wrestler/Striver with God" (from *sarah* = to fight, struggle), adopted by Keil, Kurtz, Lange, and most modern translations. The Septuagint and Vulgate render the last clause as "thou hast had power with God; much more shalt thou prevail with men."

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html

**Pentecostal (Guzik):** Jacob "moved from being defined by deception and cheating to being one who rules or struggles with God." Yet Guzik notes Jacob continued to live out both names for the rest of his life — sometimes acting like Israel, sometimes reverting to Jacob.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

**Precept Austin (Griffith-Thomas):** The new name meant a new character. "He is asked his name, and is compelled to call himself Jacob, 'Supplanter.' But this is to be changed to 'Israel,' 'God's Prince' or 'God's Perseverer' (Driver — The Book of Genesis); the one who is no longer the crafty one, but he who is worthy to prevail, to lead, to rule, to overcome." Griffith-Thomas also notes the Septuagint gloss: "Thou hast had power with God; much more shalt thou prevail with men."

- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis_devotional_commentary_2

**Reformed Baptist (Desiring God/Piper):** "Wrestling with God changed Jacob's identity. He was no longer to be known as one who received his blessing by deception. This time he received God's blessing by prevailing with God by faith." Piper compares this to Jesus restoring Peter (John 21:15–17).

- URL: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/will-you-wrestle-with-god

---

## v. 29: *"And Jacob requested, 'Please tell me your name.' But he replied, 'Why do you ask my name?' Then he blessed Jacob there."*

**Traditional reading:** Jacob's request shows boldness of faith, but the divine being refused to disclose His name — just as the angel refused Manoah (Judges 13:18), adding "seeing it is wonderful" (incomprehensible). The refusal suggests the name was beyond human comprehension, or that Jacob already had sufficient revelation through what had occurred. "Then He blessed him there" — the blessing Jacob craved was given, though the name was withheld. Ellicott notes: "probably, however, in the blessing which followed there was a clear proof that Jacob's opponent was a Divine personage."

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html

---

## v. 30: *"So Jacob named the place Peniel, saying, 'Indeed, I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared.'"*

**Traditional reading:** "Peniel" (or Penuel) means "the face of God." Jacob marveled that he saw God face to face and survived — echoing other passages where seeing God was thought to bring death (Exod 33:20; Judg 6:22; 13:22). This confirms Jacob understood his opponent was God Himself, not merely a created angel.

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html

**Precept Austin (Griffith-Thomas):** Peniel was the third and culminating revelation in Jacob's life: Bethel ("House of God" — Divine Presence), Mahanaim ("Host of God" — Divine Power), and now Peniel ("Face of God" — Divine Favor and Fellowship). "The 'Face' of God is used constantly in Scripture as a symbol of favor, friendship, fellowship."

- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis_devotional_commentary_2

---

## v. 31: *"The sun rose above him as he passed by Penuel, and he was limping because of his hip."*

**Traditional reading:** The sunrise symbolizes both a literal new day and spiritual newness — "there was sunshine within and sunshine without" (Inglis, cited in Pulpit). The limp was a permanent physical memorial of the encounter. Just as Paul had a "thorn in the flesh" (2 Cor 12:7), Jacob carried a lifelong reminder that God had conquered him. He only discovered the lameness when he tried to walk after the wrestling.

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html

**Pentecostal (Guzik):** "Jacob's permanent limp was a daily reminder that God had conquered him… This was a small price to pay for such a great gift." It was a blessed price for the victory of having stopped relying on himself.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

**Precept Austin (Griffith-Thomas):** "The sun seemed brighter than ever that morning, and the very face of nature seemed changed by reason of that vision of the face of God."

- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis_devotional_commentary_2

---

## v. 32: *"Therefore to this day the Israelites do not eat the tendon which is at the socket of the hip, because the socket of Jacob's hip was struck near that tendon."*

**Traditional reading:** The *gid hannasheh* is the sciatic nerve (*nervus ischiaticus*, also called *tendo Achillis*), the long tendon extending from the spinal cord down to the ankle. The LXX renders it "the nerve which became numb"; the Vulgate "the nerve that withered." This dietary custom is not from the Mosaic Law but is a traditional practice originating from this historical event. JFB notes: "The practice of the Jews in abstaining from eating this in the flesh of animals, is not founded on the law of Moses, but is merely a traditional." Pulpit Commentary adds: "the custom continues to the present time among the Hebrews of cutting out this sinew from the beasts they kill and eat."

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html
- URL: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/32.htm

**Ellicott (older Anglican):** "Jewish commentators notice that this was the second special ordinance imposed upon the race of Abraham, circumcision having been enjoined upon them by God, while this grew out of an historical event in the life of their progenitor, to the reality of which it bears remarkable testimony."

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html

---

## Summary of Key Protestant Differences on Genesis 32

**Nature of the Wrestling:** Reformed theologians (Calvin, Hengstenberg) tended to see the wrestling as a vision or dream; most Baptists, Pentecostals, and evangelical commentators treat it as a literal physical event with spiritual significance. The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown commentary presents both views fairly.

- URL: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/32.htm

**Identity of the Wrestler:** Most conservative Protestants (Spurgeon, Guzik, and older commentators) identify the "man" as a Christophany — a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ. Ellicott (Anglican) is more cautious: "There is no warrant for regarding the angel as an incarnation of Deity, any more than in the case of Manoah; but it was a manifestation of God mediately by His messenger."

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-32.html

**"Prevailing prayer" vs. "God conquering self":** Pentecostal/charismatic commentators (Guzik) emphasize that God wrestled Jacob to break his self-reliance — this was not primarily about "prevailing prayer." Griffith-Thomas (Precept Austin, evangelical devotional) makes this point most forcefully: "There is no lesson at all on prevailing prayer… quite the opposite." Meanwhile, some popular charismatic teaching has used this passage as a model for persistent prayer that "wrestles" with God until He blesses — though this is not the emphasis of the major sources reviewed here.

- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis_devotional_commentary_2
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-32/

**Name change and ongoing identity:** Reformed/Baptist (Piper) and devotional (Griffith-Thomas) both observe that Jacob continued to be called by his old name even after Peniel — the NT references to "Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" (not Israel) suggest Jacob did not consistently live in the new identity. This is taken as a sober warning that a high spiritual experience does not guarantee ongoing faithfulness.

- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis_devotional_commentary_2
